q: A company has a DynamoDB table with provisioned capacity of 100 RCUs. They need to perform 100 strongly consistent reads per second on items that are 8 KB each. What will happen?

opts.a: All reads will succeed without throttling
opts.b: Reads will be throttled because 200 RCUs are needed
opts.c: Reads will be throttled because 400 RCUs are needed

exp.a: 100 RCUs is insufficient for 8 KB strongly consistent reads at 100 per second.
exp.b: 8 KB / 4 KB = 2 RCUs per read. 100 reads × 2 RCUs = 200 RCUs needed. With only 100 provisioned, requests will be throttled.
exp.c: 400 RCUs would be needed for 4 RCUs per read, which is not the case for 8 KB items.
exp.d: In provisioned mode without Auto Scaling enabled, DynamoDB does not automatically increase capacity.

q: An application performs 500 eventually consistent reads per second on items of 3.5 KB each. How many RCUs should be provisioned?

opts.a: 125 RCU
opts.b: 250 RCU

exp.a: 125 RCU is half of what's needed.
exp.b: 3.5 KB rounds up to 4 KB = 1 RCU per strongly consistent read. Eventually consistent reads cost half: 0.5 RCU per read. 500 × 0.5 = 250 RCUs.
exp.c: 500 RCU would be for strongly consistent reads of 4 KB items.
exp.d: 1000 RCU is far more than needed for this scenario.

q: A DynamoDB table has a GSI that is experiencing throttling. The base table has sufficient capacity. What is the most likely cause?

opts.a: The base table's partition key has low cardinality
opts.b: The GSI has insufficient provisioned write capacity
opts.c: The table has too many LSIs

exp.a: The base table's partition key design affects base table performance, but GSI throttling is related to GSI capacity.
exp.b: GSIs have their own provisioned capacity. If the GSI write capacity is insufficient for the incoming traffic, the GSI and consequently the base table writes will be throttled.
exp.c: LSIs share capacity with the base table and don't directly impact GSI performance.
exp.d: DAX cache expiration does not cause GSI throttling.

q: A developer wants to ensure that an item is only written to DynamoDB if a specific attribute does not already exist. Which approach should they use?

opts.a: PutItem with ConditionExpression using attribute_not_exists()
opts.b: UpdateItem with FilterExpression

exp.a: PutItem with ConditionExpression 'attribute_not_exists(pk)' ensures the item is only created if the partition key doesn't exist, preventing overwrites.
exp.b: FilterExpression is for read operations, not write conditions.
exp.c: GetItem then PutItem creates a race condition and is not atomic.
exp.d: BatchWriteItem does not support ConditionExpressions.

q: Which conflict resolution strategy does DynamoDB Global Tables use when the same item is modified in two regions simultaneously?

opts.a: First-writer-wins
opts.b: Last-writer-wins based on timestamp
opts.d: The write is rejected in both regions

exp.a: First-writer-wins is not the conflict resolution strategy used by Global Tables.
exp.b: DynamoDB Global Tables uses a last-writer-wins strategy based on the timestamp of the write operation.
exp.c: No manual intervention is required; conflict resolution is automatic.
exp.d: Writes are not rejected; one will eventually win based on timestamp.

q: An application needs to read 10 items simultaneously from DynamoDB, each item is 350 KB. Which operation is most efficient?

opts.a: 10 individual GetItem calls
opts.b: A single BatchGetItem call

exp.a: 10 individual GetItem calls require 10 separate API calls with higher latency.
exp.b: BatchGetItem retrieves up to 100 items in a single API call, reducing round trips and improving efficiency.
exp.c: Query requires items to share the same partition key and cannot retrieve arbitrary items.
exp.d: Scan reads the entire table and is the least efficient option.

q: A DynamoDB table uses a partition key of 'UserID' and stores 500 million items. Queries are becoming slow. What is the most likely issue?

opts.a: The table has reached its storage limit
opts.b: Hot partition due to uneven access patterns on certain UserIDs
opts.c: DynamoDB does not support tables this large
opts.d: Too many GSIs on the table

exp.a: DynamoDB has virtually unlimited storage and doesn't have a table storage limit.
exp.b: If certain UserIDs are accessed much more frequently (celebrity users, popular accounts), their partitions become hot, causing throttling.
exp.c: DynamoDB supports tables with billions of items.
exp.d: While too many GSIs can impact write performance, query slowness on the base table suggests hot partitions.

q: Which DynamoDB feature should you use to aggregate item changes and send them to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose for analytics?

opts.a: DynamoDB Export to S3
opts.b: DynamoDB Streams with Lambda forwarding to Firehose
opts.c: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB

exp.a: Export to S3 is for point-in-time exports, not real-time streaming to Firehose.
exp.b: While this works, it adds Lambda complexity. Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB is more direct.
exp.c: Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB captures changes and can be directly connected to Kinesis Data Firehose for analytics without Lambda.
exp.d: Contributor Insights identifies hot keys but doesn't stream data to Firehose.

q: A table has a composite primary key (UserID, Timestamp). A query needs all items for UserID='U123' between two dates. Which approach is correct?

opts.a: Scan with FilterExpression on UserID and Timestamp
opts.b: Query with KeyConditionExpression using partition key and sort key range

exp.a: Scan reads the entire table and is inefficient for this use case.
exp.b: Query with KeyConditionExpression: UserID = 'U123' AND Timestamp BETWEEN date1 AND date2 efficiently retrieves only matching items.
exp.c: GetItem retrieves a single item; it cannot retrieve a range of items.
exp.d: BatchGetItem requires knowing exact keys and is impractical for time ranges.

q: What is the behavior of DAX when a write operation occurs?

opts.a: Write-around: writes go directly to DynamoDB, bypassing DAX
opts.b: Write-through: writes are sent to both DAX and DynamoDB simultaneously
opts.c: Write-back: writes go to DAX first, then asynchronously to DynamoDB
opts.d: Write-invalidate: DAX invalidates the cache entry and writes to DynamoDB

exp.a: DAX does not bypass writes; it uses write-through caching.
exp.b: DAX uses write-through caching: writes are written to DynamoDB first, and the item cache is updated simultaneously.
exp.c: Write-back would risk data loss and is not used by DAX.
exp.d: DAX updates the item cache, not just invalidates it.

q: A developer needs to atomically increment a counter in DynamoDB without reading the current value first. Which operation should they use?

opts.a: GetItem then PutItem
opts.b: UpdateItem with SET expression

exp.a: GetItem then PutItem is not atomic and creates race conditions.
exp.b: SET requires knowing the current value to set the new value.
exp.c: UpdateItem with ADD atomically increments a numeric attribute without needing to read the current value first.
exp.d: TransactWriteItems provides transactions but is overkill for simple atomic counters.

q: An e-commerce application needs to transfer funds between two accounts in DynamoDB. Which feature ensures both updates succeed or neither does?

opts.a: BatchWriteItem
opts.b: DynamoDB Transactions (TransactWriteItems)

exp.a: BatchWriteItem is not atomic across items; individual items can fail independently.
exp.b: TransactWriteItems provides all-or-nothing (ACID) guarantees across multiple items, ensuring both debit and credit succeed or neither does.
exp.c: Conditional PutItem only applies to a single item and cannot ensure atomicity across two items.
exp.d: DynamoDB Streams captures changes but doesn't provide transactional guarantees.

q: What is the impact on WCUs when writing to a DynamoDB table that has 3 Global Secondary Indexes?

opts.a: No additional WCU cost for GSIs
opts.b: Each GSI consumes its own WCUs when the indexed attributes are modified
opts.c: Total WCU cost is always 4x (base table + 3 GSIs)
opts.d: GSIs only consume WCUs during index backfilling

exp.a: GSIs do consume WCUs when data changes affect indexed attributes.
exp.b: Each GSI has its own provisioned WCUs. When a write to the base table includes attributes that are part of a GSI's key or projected attributes, that GSI consumes its own WCUs.
exp.c: Not every write affects all GSIs; only writes that change indexed/projected attributes consume GSI WCUs.
exp.d: GSIs consume WCUs for all ongoing writes that affect them, not just during backfilling.

q: A DynamoDB table needs to support queries by both 'email' and 'phone number' as alternate lookup keys. The table's primary key is 'UserID'. What should you do?

opts.a: Create two LSIs with email and phone as sort keys
opts.b: Create two GSIs: one with email as partition key and one with phone as partition key
opts.c: Create a composite primary key with email and phone

exp.a: LSIs share the same partition key as the base table (UserID), so they can't enable lookups by email or phone alone.
exp.b: GSIs allow completely different partition keys, enabling efficient lookups by email and phone number independently.
exp.c: Changing the primary key doesn't solve the need for multiple alternate lookup patterns.
exp.d: Scan with FilterExpression reads the entire table and is highly inefficient.

q: What is the maximum size of a single Scan or Query response before pagination is required?

opts.a: 256 KB
opts.b: 1 MB

exp.a: 256 KB is too small; DynamoDB returns more data per response.
exp.b: A single Query or Scan response can return up to 1 MB of data. If more data exists, LastEvaluatedKey is returned for pagination.
exp.c: 4 MB is the transaction limit, not the Query/Scan response limit.
exp.d: 16 MB is the BatchGetItem limit, not the Query/Scan response limit.

q: A company wants to ensure their DynamoDB table is protected against accidental deletion. Which feature should they enable?

opts.a: DynamoDB Streams
opts.b: Deletion Protection

exp.a: DynamoDB Streams captures data changes but doesn't protect against table deletion.
exp.b: DynamoDB Deletion Protection prevents a table from being accidentally deleted. It must be disabled before the table can be deleted.
exp.c: TTL is for automatic item expiration, not table protection.
exp.d: DAX is a caching layer and doesn't protect tables from deletion.

q: You are designing a leaderboard system. Players have scores that change frequently, and you need to query top 10 players. Which design is most efficient?

opts.a: Table with PlayerID as partition key and use Scan to find top 10
opts.b: GSI with a fixed partition key (e.g., 'GAME#1') and Score as sort key, query in descending order with Limit 10
opts.c: Store top 10 in a separate table updated by Lambda
opts.d: Use DAX to cache all player scores

exp.a: Scan reads the entire table every time and is highly inefficient for leaderboard queries.
exp.b: Using a GSI with a fixed partition key groups all players together, and a sort key on Score allows efficient top-N queries with ScanIndexForward=false and Limit=10.
exp.c: While this works, it adds complexity with Lambda and additional tables; the GSI approach is simpler.
exp.d: DAX caches individual reads but doesn't solve the problem of efficiently querying top scores.

q: What is the difference between DynamoDB 'Query' with FilterExpression and 'Query' with KeyConditionExpression?

opts.a: Both reduce the RCU consumption equally
opts.b: KeyConditionExpression reduces data read from storage; FilterExpression filters after data is read
opts.c: FilterExpression is applied before data is read; KeyConditionExpression is applied after

exp.a: Only KeyConditionExpression reduces the amount of data read and thus RCU consumption.
exp.b: KeyConditionExpression determines which items are read from the partition (reducing I/O), while FilterExpression is applied after items are read (RCUs already consumed).
exp.c: This is reversed; KeyConditionExpression is applied first to determine what to read.
exp.d: They serve different purposes and are applied at different stages.

q: A table has a partition key 'Country' with values like 'US', 'UK', 'IN'. Approximately 80% of traffic goes to 'US'. What is the best strategy?

opts.a: Increase the overall provisioned capacity
opts.b: Use write sharding by appending a random suffix to the partition key (e.g., US_1, US_2, US_3)

exp.a: Increasing capacity doesn't solve the hot partition problem; US partition will still be throttled.
exp.b: Write sharding distributes the 'US' traffic across multiple partitions (US_1, US_2, etc.), eliminating the hot partition issue.
exp.c: On-demand mode still has per-partition limits and won't fully solve hot partition issues.
exp.d: Adding a GSI doesn't solve the hot partition problem on the base table.

q: Which UpdateExpression action removes an attribute from a DynamoDB item?

opts.a: DELETE
opts.b: REMOVE

exp.a: DELETE is used to remove elements from a Set data type, not to remove an attribute entirely.
exp.b: REMOVE removes one or more attributes from an item entirely.
exp.c: DROP is not a valid UpdateExpression action in DynamoDB.
exp.d: UNSET is not a valid UpdateExpression action in DynamoDB.

q: What are the valid UpdateExpression actions in DynamoDB?

opts.a: SET, REMOVE, ADD, DELETE
opts.b: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT

exp.a: The four valid UpdateExpression actions are SET (modify/add), REMOVE (remove attributes), ADD (add to number or set), and DELETE (remove from set).
exp.b: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT are SQL commands, not DynamoDB UpdateExpression actions.
exp.c: GET is not an UpdateExpression action; it's a separate read operation.
exp.d: PUT and DROP are not valid UpdateExpression actions.

q: An application is using DAX for read caching. After updating an item, the application still reads stale data. What is the most likely cause?

opts.a: DAX write-through failed
opts.b: The application is reading from the DAX query cache which was not invalidated
opts.c: DynamoDB has not replicated the write
opts.d: The table is in on-demand mode

exp.a: DAX write-through updates the item cache, but may not invalidate query cache entries.
exp.b: DAX maintains separate item and query caches. Write-through updates the item cache, but the query cache may still contain stale results until its TTL expires.
exp.c: DynamoDB writes are immediately consistent within a region for the base table.
exp.d: Capacity mode does not affect DAX caching behavior.

q: Which DynamoDB feature allows you to create an exact copy of a table for testing without impacting production?

opts.a: DynamoDB Streams
opts.b: On-demand backup and restore to a new table

exp.a: DynamoDB Streams captures changes but doesn't create a table copy directly.
exp.b: On-demand backup allows you to create a backup and restore it to a new table name, creating an exact copy without impacting the source table.
exp.c: Global Tables creates replicas across regions for high availability, not for testing purposes.
exp.d: DAX is a cache and does not create table copies.

q: What is the behavior of DynamoDB when a partition's 10 GB storage limit is reached?

opts.a: The table becomes read-only
opts.b: DynamoDB automatically splits the partition

exp.a: The table does not become read-only when a partition fills up.
exp.b: When a partition approaches or reaches 10 GB, DynamoDB automatically splits it into two new partitions to distribute the data.
exp.c: Writes are not permanently rejected; partition splitting handles growth.
exp.d: DynamoDB never automatically deletes a table.

q: You need to perform 30 transactional reads per second on items of 8 KB each. How many RCUs are required?

opts.a: 60 RCU
opts.b: 120 RCU

exp.a: 60 RCU doesn't account for the transactional overhead.
exp.b: 8 KB / 4 KB = 2 RCUs per strongly consistent read. Transactional = 2 × 2 = 4 RCUs per read. 30 × 4 = 120 RCUs.
exp.c: 240 RCU would be for 60 transactional reads, not 30.
exp.d: 480 RCU is far more than needed.

q: A DynamoDB table uses On-Demand capacity. What is the initial throughput for a newly created table?

opts.a: Unlimited from the start
opts.b: Up to 40,000 RCUs and 40,000 WCUs

exp.a: On-demand is not unlimited from the start; it has initial limits that scale up.
exp.b: 40,000 is the account-level default limit, not the initial table throughput.
exp.c: A new on-demand table can handle up to 4,000 RCUs and 4,000 WCUs immediately. It scales up as traffic increases.
exp.d: 100 is too low; newly created on-demand tables support higher initial throughput.

q: What is the maximum previous peak that DynamoDB On-Demand mode can instantly accommodate?

opts.a: Equal to the previous peak
opts.b: Up to double the previous peak

exp.a: On-demand can handle more than just the previous peak.
exp.b: DynamoDB On-Demand can instantly accommodate up to double (2x) the previous peak traffic. Beyond that, throttling may occur until capacity scales further.
exp.c: 5x exceeds the instant scaling capability.
exp.d: 10x exceeds the instant scaling capability.

q: How does DynamoDB handle the 'fetch' operation when a projected attribute in a GSI is not available?

opts.a: Returns null for the attribute
opts.b: Performs a 'fetch' back to the base table, consuming additional RCUs
opts.d: Returns the item without the attribute

exp.a: DynamoDB can retrieve the attribute from the base table, not return null.
exp.b: If you request attributes not projected into the GSI, DynamoDB fetches them from the base table, consuming additional RCUs from the base table.
exp.c: DynamoDB does not throw an error; it fetches from the base table.
exp.d: For Query/Scan on GSI, non-projected attributes are fetched from the base table if requested.

q: Which scenario best suits DynamoDB On-Demand capacity mode?

opts.a: Steady, predictable traffic with consistent load 24/7
opts.b: Unpredictable traffic with spiky workloads and new applications with unknown patterns
opts.c: Very low traffic that never changes

exp.a: Steady traffic is better served by provisioned capacity with reserved capacity for cost savings.
exp.b: On-demand is ideal for unpredictable, spiky workloads and new applications where traffic patterns are unknown.
exp.c: Very low, stable traffic could use provisioned capacity at minimum settings for lower cost.
exp.d: Reserved capacity is only available with provisioned mode, not on-demand.

q: A developer enables DynamoDB Streams on a table and configures a Lambda function as a consumer. The Lambda function fails processing a record. What happens?

opts.a: The failed record is skipped and processing continues
opts.b: Lambda retries the entire batch until it succeeds or the record expires from the stream (24 hours)
opts.d: Only the failed record is retried individually

exp.a: By default, failed records are not skipped; Lambda retries the batch.
exp.b: Lambda retries the entire batch of records until successful processing or until the records expire from DynamoDB Streams (24 hours). This can block processing of new records.
exp.c: Streams are never automatically disabled due to consumer failures.
exp.d: Lambda processes records in batches; it retries the entire batch, not individual records (unless configured with bisect batch on error).

q: How can you prevent a Lambda function from being blocked by a poison pill record in DynamoDB Streams?

opts.a: Increase Lambda timeout
opts.b: Configure 'Maximum retry attempts' and 'On-failure destination' (e.g., SQS dead-letter queue)

exp.a: Increasing timeout doesn't solve the poison pill problem; the record will still fail.
exp.b: Configuring maximum retry attempts limits retries, and an on-failure destination (DLQ) captures failed records for later analysis without blocking the stream.
exp.c: Disabling streams removes all real-time processing capability.
exp.d: Increasing retention doesn't prevent blocking; it actually extends the blocking duration.

q: What is the 'BisectBatchOnFunctionError' feature in Lambda's DynamoDB Streams event source mapping?

opts.a: It splits the Lambda function into two instances
opts.b: It splits the failing batch into two smaller batches and retries each separately to isolate the problematic record
opts.d: It cuts the Lambda timeout in half

exp.a: It does not split the Lambda function; it splits the batch of records.
exp.b: BisectBatchOnFunctionError splits a failing batch in half and retries each sub-batch, progressively isolating the problematic record(s).
exp.c: It does not duplicate records; it splits batches for retry purposes.
exp.d: It has nothing to do with Lambda timeout.

q: You want to use DynamoDB to store user profiles where each user has a different set of attributes. Which DynamoDB characteristic makes this possible?

opts.a: Secondary indexes
opts.b: Schema-less nature (flexible schema)

exp.a: Secondary indexes enable alternate query patterns, not flexible schemas.
exp.b: DynamoDB is schema-less beyond the primary key; each item can have different attributes, making it ideal for varying user profile structures.
exp.c: Streams capture data changes, not related to schema flexibility.
exp.d: Consistency relates to read behavior, not schema structure.

q: A table has an LSI with projection type 'KEYS_ONLY'. A query on the LSI requests a non-key attribute. What happens?

opts.a: The query fails with an error
opts.b: DynamoDB fetches the attribute from the base table (at additional RCU cost)
opts.c: NULL is returned for that attribute
opts.d: The attribute is automatically added to the LSI projection

exp.a: The query does not fail; DynamoDB can still retrieve the attribute.
exp.b: For LSIs, DynamoDB performs a 'fetch' back to the base table to retrieve non-projected attributes, consuming additional RCUs.
exp.c: DynamoDB retrieves the actual value, not NULL.
exp.d: Projections are not automatically modified.

q: What is the difference between GSI fetch behavior and LSI fetch behavior for non-projected attributes?

opts.a: Both GSI and LSI can fetch from the base table
opts.b: LSIs can fetch from base table; GSIs cannot return non-projected attributes at all
opts.c: GSIs fetch from the base table; LSIs cannot

exp.a: Only LSIs can fetch from the base table; GSIs cannot.
exp.b: LSIs can fetch non-projected attributes from the base table because they share the same partition. GSIs cannot; you can only get attributes that are projected into the GSI.
exp.c: This is reversed; LSIs can fetch, GSIs cannot.
exp.d: LSIs can fetch non-projected attributes from the base table.

q: A DynamoDB table receives 1000 writes per second with items averaging 0.5 KB. The table has 2 GSIs that index all items. What is the minimum WCU needed for the base table alone?

opts.a: 500 WCU
opts.b: 1000 WCU

exp.a: 500 WCU is insufficient; 0.5 KB rounds up to 1 KB = 1 WCU per write.
exp.b: 0.5 KB rounds up to 1 KB = 1 WCU per write. 1000 writes × 1 WCU = 1000 WCUs for the base table. GSIs have separate capacity.
exp.c: 2000 WCU would be base table + 1 GSI combined, but the question asks for base table alone.
exp.d: 3000 WCU would be base table + 2 GSIs combined.

q: What is DynamoDB's behavior when using ExpressionAttributeNames in queries?

opts.a: It creates new attributes in the table
opts.b: It provides name substitution for reserved words and special characters in expressions
opts.d: It creates aliases for table names

exp.a: ExpressionAttributeNames does not create new attributes.
exp.b: ExpressionAttributeNames provides placeholder substitution (e.g., #s for 'status') when attribute names are DynamoDB reserved words or contain special characters.
exp.c: It does not encrypt anything; it's for name substitution in expressions.
exp.d: It substitutes attribute names, not table names.

q: What is the purpose of ExpressionAttributeValues in DynamoDB operations?

opts.a: To define default values for new attributes
opts.b: To provide value substitution placeholders in condition and filter expressions
opts.d: To define data types for attributes

exp.a: ExpressionAttributeValues doesn't define default values for attributes.
exp.b: ExpressionAttributeValues provides value placeholders (e.g., :val1) in expressions, allowing you to specify comparison values safely.
exp.c: It does not perform encryption.
exp.d: While values include type information, the primary purpose is substitution in expressions.

q: A company needs to process DynamoDB Streams with exactly-once semantics. Which approach should they consider?

opts.a: Use Lambda with DynamoDB Streams (at-least-once by default)
opts.b: Make the Lambda function idempotent so duplicate processing has no side effects

exp.a: Lambda with DynamoDB Streams provides at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once.
exp.b: Since DynamoDB Streams guarantees at-least-once delivery, making the processing function idempotent ensures that duplicate records don't cause incorrect results, effectively achieving exactly-once semantics.
exp.c: SQS doesn't provide exactly-once semantics by default either (except FIFO with deduplication).
exp.d: Stream retention cannot be changed from 24 hours and doesn't solve the semantics issue.

q: A multi-tenant application stores data for 10,000 tenants. Which partition key design prevents hot partitions while enabling efficient per-tenant queries?

opts.a: Use 'TENANT' as partition key for all items
opts.b: Use TenantID as partition key
opts.c: Use a composite key of TenantID#random_suffix as partition key
opts.d: Use a sequential numeric ID as partition key

exp.a: Using the same value for all items creates a massive hot partition.
exp.b: Using TenantID as partition key distributes data across tenants and enables efficient queries for each tenant's data.
exp.c: Random suffix makes it difficult to query all items for a single tenant efficiently.
exp.d: Sequential IDs can create hot partitions if most writes go to recent IDs.

q: What happens to LSIs when the 10 GB item collection size limit is reached?

opts.a: The LSI is automatically deleted
opts.b: Writes that would exceed the limit are rejected with ItemCollectionSizeLimitExceededException
opts.c: DynamoDB automatically creates a new partition

exp.a: LSIs are never automatically deleted.
exp.b: When the total size of items sharing a partition key (across the table and all LSIs) exceeds 10 GB, DynamoDB rejects further writes with ItemCollectionSizeLimitExceededException.
exp.c: The 10 GB limit is per partition key collection when LSIs exist; it's not resolved by partition splitting.
exp.d: LSIs don't stop updating; writes are rejected entirely.

q: Which DynamoDB operation should you use to check if an item exists without consuming full read capacity for large items?

opts.a: GetItem with ProjectionExpression returning only the key
opts.b: Query with Limit 1

exp.a: GetItem with ProjectionExpression to return only the key attributes minimizes data returned, though RCUs are still based on item size (minimum 4 KB). However, it's the most targeted approach.
exp.b: Query with Limit 1 works but is more suited for composite keys with sort key conditions.
exp.c: Scan reads the entire table and is extremely inefficient for existence checks.
exp.d: DescribeTable returns table metadata, not item existence information.

q: What is the maximum batch size (number of records) that Lambda can receive from DynamoDB Streams in a single invocation?

exp.a: 100 is the default batch size, but not the maximum.
exp.b: 1,000 is below the maximum configurable batch size.
exp.c: The maximum batch size for Lambda reading from DynamoDB Streams is 10,000 records per invocation.
exp.d: 100,000 exceeds the maximum batch size limit.

q: A DynamoDB table has Auto Scaling configured with target utilization of 70%. What does this mean?

opts.a: Auto Scaling triggers when consumed capacity reaches 70% of provisioned capacity
opts.b: 70% of requests will succeed
opts.c: The table will always use 70% of maximum capacity
opts.d: 30% of capacity is reserved for burst traffic

exp.a: Auto Scaling adjusts provisioned capacity to maintain approximately 70% utilization, scaling up when consumption approaches this target.
exp.b: Target utilization is about capacity management, not request success rate.
exp.c: The table doesn't always use 70%; this is the target around which capacity is managed.
exp.d: While there is effectively headroom, it's not explicitly reserved for burst.

q: You need to store a DynamoDB item that contains a nested JSON structure 5 levels deep. Is this supported?

opts.a: No, DynamoDB only supports flat key-value pairs
opts.b: Yes, using Map and List data types with up to 32 levels of nesting
opts.c: Yes, but only up to 3 levels of nesting

exp.a: DynamoDB supports complex nested data structures using Map and List types.
exp.b: DynamoDB supports nesting using Map and List data types up to 32 levels deep. 5 levels is well within this limit.
exp.c: DynamoDB supports much more than 3 levels of nesting.
exp.d: Nesting is limited to 32 levels, not unlimited.

q: What is the maximum nesting depth for DynamoDB document types (Maps and Lists)?

opts.a: 8 levels
opts.b: 16 levels

exp.a: 8 levels is below the actual maximum nesting depth.
exp.b: 16 levels is below the actual maximum nesting depth.
exp.c: DynamoDB supports a maximum nesting depth of 32 levels for document type attributes.
exp.d: 64 levels exceeds the DynamoDB nesting limit.

q: An application requires reading the same DynamoDB item thousands of times per second. Which solution provides the best performance?

opts.a: Increase RCUs on the base table
opts.b: Use DynamoDB DAX for microsecond latency cached reads
opts.c: Use Global Tables across all regions

exp.a: Increasing RCUs helps but still limited to per-partition throughput of 3000 RCU.
exp.b: DAX provides microsecond response times for repeated reads of the same item by caching it in memory, dramatically reducing load on DynamoDB.
exp.c: Global Tables is for multi-region availability, not for improving read performance of a single item.
exp.d: GSIs provide alternate query patterns but don't cache frequently accessed items.

q: What is the consistency behavior of DAX for read operations?

opts.a: DAX always provides strongly consistent reads
opts.b: DAX provides eventually consistent reads from cache; strongly consistent reads bypass DAX and go directly to DynamoDB
opts.c: DAX provides both strongly and eventually consistent reads from cache

exp.a: DAX does not provide strongly consistent reads from cache.
exp.b: DAX serves eventually consistent reads from its cache. If you request a strongly consistent read, DAX passes the request directly to DynamoDB, bypassing the cache.
exp.c: DAX cannot guarantee strong consistency from cache.
exp.d: DAX primarily caches read operations, with write-through for writes.

q: Which scenario would make DynamoDB a poor choice compared to Amazon RDS?

opts.a: Storing session data with high throughput requirements
opts.b: Complex multi-table JOIN operations with ACID transactions across many tables
opts.d: Storing IoT sensor data with time-series patterns

exp.a: Session data with high throughput is an ideal DynamoDB use case.
exp.b: Complex JOIN operations across many tables are better served by relational databases like RDS. DynamoDB doesn't support JOINs.
exp.c: Key-value lookups are DynamoDB's primary strength.
exp.d: IoT time-series data with partition key (device ID) and sort key (timestamp) works well in DynamoDB.

q: What is the maximum number of concurrent DynamoDB Streams consumers for a single shard?

exp.a: More than 1 consumer can read from a DynamoDB stream shard simultaneously.
exp.b: A DynamoDB stream shard supports a maximum of 2 simultaneous readers/consumers to avoid throttling.
exp.c: 5 simultaneous readers would exceed the shard read capacity.
exp.d: There is a limit of 2 concurrent readers per shard.

q: You have a DynamoDB table with a composite key (PK: CustomerID, SK: OrderID). You want to query all orders for a customer sorted by order date. What should you do?

opts.a: Create a LSI with OrderDate as the sort key
opts.b: Create a GSI with CustomerID as partition key and OrderDate as sort key
opts.c: Both A and B would work

exp.a: An LSI with OrderDate as sort key would work since LSIs share the same partition key (CustomerID).
exp.b: A GSI with CustomerID as partition key and OrderDate as sort key would also work.
exp.c: Both approaches work. LSI must be created at table creation and shares throughput; GSI can be added later with independent capacity.
exp.d: Scan is inefficient and reads the entire table.

q: What is the purpose of the 'ReturnConsumedCapacity' parameter in DynamoDB requests?

opts.a: To limit the capacity consumed by the request
opts.b: To return information about how much capacity was consumed by the request
opts.c: To reserve capacity for future requests
opts.d: To throttle the request if capacity is insufficient

exp.a: This parameter doesn't limit capacity consumption.
exp.b: ReturnConsumedCapacity returns detailed information about the capacity units consumed by the operation (TOTAL, INDEXES, or NONE).
exp.c: It doesn't reserve capacity; it reports consumption after the fact.
exp.d: Throttling happens automatically based on provisioned capacity, not due to this parameter.

q: What is the 'ReturnValues' parameter used for in DynamoDB write operations?

opts.a: To validate input data
opts.b: To return the item's attribute values before or after the operation
opts.c: To specify which table to write to

exp.a: ReturnValues doesn't validate input data.
exp.b: ReturnValues specifies whether to return the item attributes before (ALL_OLD, UPDATED_OLD) or after (ALL_NEW, UPDATED_NEW) the modification, or NONE.
exp.c: The table is specified in the TableName parameter, not ReturnValues.
exp.d: Encryption is configured at the table level, not per-operation.

q: A DynamoDB table with On-Demand capacity experiences a sudden traffic spike of 10x the normal load within seconds. What is the expected behavior?

opts.a: All requests succeed immediately
opts.b: Some requests may be throttled initially until DynamoDB scales up
opts.d: DynamoDB automatically converts to provisioned mode

exp.a: Not all requests will necessarily succeed during an extreme sudden spike.
exp.b: On-demand can instantly handle up to 2x the previous peak. Beyond that, some throttling may occur while DynamoDB scales to accommodate the new traffic level.
exp.c: DynamoDB does not crash; it is highly resilient.
exp.d: DynamoDB never automatically converts between capacity modes.

q: Which DynamoDB feature helps you understand the access patterns of your table to optimize cost?

opts.a: DynamoDB Contributor Insights
opts.b: AWS Cost Explorer with DynamoDB filters

exp.a: Contributor Insights identifies frequently accessed keys and throttled items.
exp.b: Cost Explorer shows DynamoDB spending trends and cost breakdown.
exp.c: CloudWatch metrics show actual capacity consumption patterns.
exp.d: All three tools together provide comprehensive insight into access patterns and cost optimization opportunities.

q: What is the DynamoDB burst capacity feature?

opts.a: A paid add-on for extra capacity during traffic spikes
opts.b: DynamoDB retains up to 5 minutes of unused read/write capacity for occasional bursts
opts.c: An automatic switch to on-demand mode during bursts
opts.d: A reserved pool of 10,000 extra RCUs/WCUs

exp.a: Burst capacity is not a paid add-on; it's included automatically.
exp.b: DynamoDB retains up to 5 minutes (300 seconds) of unused provisioned capacity that can be consumed during short traffic bursts.
exp.c: DynamoDB does not automatically switch capacity modes.
exp.d: Burst capacity is based on unused provisioned capacity, not a fixed pool.
